summary: Clarifies the standards status of the documents that define forward and reverse mapping of IPv6 addresses in the DNS. It moves the A6 record and bit-string label specifications to experimental status. It updates RFCs 2673 and 2874 and was later updated by RFC 6672.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo resolves a standards-status question about ways to represent IPv6 addresses in DNS. It recommends AAAA for production at the time and moves A6 and binary labels to Experimental status.

questions: what happened to the a6 record
how are ipv6 addresses stored in dns
subtitle: A standards-status decision on AAAA, A6, and bit-label approaches for IPv6 in DNS.

tldr.problem: Two proposed ways to represent IPv6 addresses in DNS created uncertainty about which approach to use for deployment.
tldr.mechanism: The memo recommends AAAA for production use at the time and moves the A6 and binary-label specifications to Experimental status.
tldr.outcome: It also states that DNAME use in the IPv6 reverse tree should be deprecated and was later updated by RFC 6672.

today: RFC 3363 is an Informational RFC published in August 2002. It updates RFCs 2673 and 2874 and was later updated by RFC 6672.

sections.title: Why a Decision Was Needed
sections.content:
The IETF had two proposed-standard approaches for IPv6 address records in DNS: AAAA and A6. The memo says having both choices caused confusion about which to deploy and could delay IPv6 deployment.

This document summarizes the outcome of technical discussions in the relevant working groups. It changes the status of RFC 2673 and RFC 2874 from Proposed Standard to Experimental.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different record types had been proposed for IPv6 addresses, and people were unsure which one to deploy. This memo records the working groups’ decision about their status.

sections.title: AAAA and A6 Records
sections.content:
The working-group chairs’ understanding of the consensus was that AAAA records were preferable for production deployment at that time. A6 records had useful properties, but the costs and risks were not yet understood well enough.

A6 can build an address through chains of records. The memo was concerned that each additional lookup could add time and create another chance for resolution to fail. It therefore recommended keeping RFC 1886 on the standards track and moving RFC 2874 to Experimental status.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo favored AAAA for production at the time because an A6 address could require a chain of lookups. It said the benefits and risks of A6 needed more study.

sections.title: Binary Labels and the Reverse Tree
sections.content:
RFC 2673 defined binary labels for DNS. The memo says deployment of a new label type is difficult because servers that do not support it reject queries containing it. It also says the hexadecimal text form of IPv6 addresses appeared sufficient for expected reverse-DNS delegation schemes, so RFC 2673 moved to Experimental status.

The memo links the use of DNAME in the IPv6 reverse tree to the need for fragmented A6 addresses in the main tree. Its intent was that DNAME use in the reverse tree be deprecated along with the move of RFC 2874 to Experimental status.
sections.plainLanguage: Older DNS servers may reject the new binary label type, and the memo considered it unnecessary for reverse mapping. It also intended to deprecate DNAME in the reverse tree as part of the A6 decision.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The memo does not specify a protocol, so it identifies no direct security considerations. It notes that the relationship between A6 and DNSSEC was not well understood in the community and that choosing AAAA led to a DNSSEC model for IPv6 that paralleled then-current IPv4 practice.

The document requires no IANA action.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo changes the status of DNS specifications rather than defining a new protocol. It records one indirect security consideration and asks IANA to take no action.
